blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums`, move every `0` to the end while keeping the **relative order** of the non-zero elements. You must do it **in place**, without making a copy of the array.

blocks.alt: Before: [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]. After: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]. The non-zero values keep their order and the zeroes collect at the end.

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]
Output: [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]

Input:  nums = [0]
Output: [0]

blocks.text: Two rules make this more than a sort: the non-zero values must stay in their **original order** (1, then 3, then 12), and the work must happen **inside the same array**. Sorting would scramble the order, and building a second array breaks the in-place rule.
Brute force: use a second array
Copy the non-zero values into a new array, fill the rest with zeroes, then copy everything back.

That is **O(n)** time, but it needs **O(n) extra space** for the copy. Another brute force — shifting everything left whenever you meet a zero — avoids the copy but costs **O(n²)** because of all the shifting.
The key insight: a reader and a writer

Use two indexes moving through the same array. `read` looks at every element once. `write` points at the next slot where a non-zero value should go. Whenever `read` finds a non-zero value, swap it into `write` and move `write` forward.
At every moment, everything **before** `write` is finished: non-zero values in their original order. Everything between `write` and `read` is a zero waiting to be pushed back.

blocks.alt: Snapshots of move zeroes on [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]. Each time the read pointer finds a non-zero value it is swapped to the write pointer, and write moves one step right. Finished cells are blue.

blocks.alt: Extra array: O(n) time and O(n) space. Two pointers: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: `read` visits each element once and every swap is O(1): **O(n) time, O(1) extra space**.

items: **Zeroes already at the end** — `[1, 2, 0]` is untouched.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

The reader/writer pair is the workhorse of in-place array problems: removing every copy of a value, removing duplicates from a sorted array (the next problem), and partitioning an array around a pivot in quicksort all use it. Whenever a problem says **in place** and asks you to keep some elements and drop others, reach for it first.
